Rainbow smelt (Osmerus mordax) deposits small, spherical, demersal eggs that adhere to gravel or vegetation in freshwater streams and estuaries. The mean egg diameter has been measured at 0.26 cm [Lb = 0.26 cm], a size that falls within the typical range for anadromous osmerids and influences early larval yolk reserves. Incubation duration is strongly temperature-dependent; laboratory trials conducted at a stable temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C] indicate that hatching occurs after approximately 27 days [ab = approximately 27 days], a period that allows for significant embryonic development of the digestive tract and circulatory system prior to chorion rupture. Upon eclosion, the newly emerged prolarva is lecithotrophic and carries a substantial yolk sac. The wet weight at birth was determined from volumetric egg measurements to be 0.00022 grams [Wwb = 0.00022 grams], corresponding to the small maternal investment per offspring typical of broadcast spawners that produce large numbers of eggs. This initial mass constrains the duration of the endogenous feeding phase, after which the exotrophic transition depends on the seasonal onset of zooplankton blooms.

As the yolk-sac larva undergoes yolk absorption and progresses toward the onset of exogenous feeding, somatic growth accelerates rapidly under appropriate thermal regimes. Field surveys and mark-recapture studies have provided detailed information on the species' maximum attainable size. The ultimate total length recorded for Osmerus mordax is 35.6 cm [Li = 35.6 cm], a value typically reached by the oldest and largest individuals in northern populations where growing seasons are shorter. This maximum length is notably larger than that observed in congeneric species from Atlantic drainages, reflecting the relatively productive foraging grounds available in some Great Lakes tributaries. Growth trajectories are influenced by water temperature, prey density, and intraspecific competition, with faster initial growth often correlated with earlier attainment of reproductive size. The species exhibits indeterminate growth, though length increments diminish markedly after sexual maturation. Most adult smelt in exploited populations rarely approach this asymptotic length because size-selective mortality from commercial and recreational fisheries truncates the older age classes and removes the largest individuals before senescence.

Reproductive maturation in Osmerus mordax is closely linked to both body size and thermal history during the juvenile period. The total length at puberty has been estimated at 19.5 cm [Lp = 19.5 cm], a threshold that corresponds to the minimum size at which females initiate vitellogenesis and males develop functional gonads. Individuals achieving this length typically do so during their second or third growing season, depending on local growth rates. At the temperature regime commonly experienced by maturing smelt in their nursery habitats, 16.5 °C [T = 16.5 °C], the age at first reproduction has been documented at 730 days after hatching [tR = 730 days after hatching], meaning that most fish spawn for the first time in the spring of their second year. This relatively early maturation compared to body size reflects the species' annual life cycle and the strong selective pressure to reproduce before winter mortality increases. The relationship between length and maturity is not absolute, as some fast-growing young-of-year may reach puberty during their first autumn, though such early maturation is rare and energetically costly.

Under optimal thermal conditions of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the maximum reproductive output of Osmerus mordax has been characterized in terms of both fecundity per event and spawning frequency. Adult females produce approximately 123 eggs per spawning event, and the same individuals may complete one spawning act annually. The estimated daily reproduction rate reaches approximately 123 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 123 eggs per day], given the short window of suitable stream temperatures. This annual spawning activity is typical of iteroparous anadromous populations, though some landlocked stocks exhibit a semelparous tendency after a single, more fecund event. The trade-off between egg size and egg number is evident; the 0.26 cm egg diameter constrains the total volume of the clutch that can be accommodated within the body cavity. The observed fecundity, when multiplied by the annual spawning frequency, yields an estimated daily reproduction rate that is modest compared to obligate semelparous salmonids, but sustainable over multiple years within a lifetime.

Longevity data from otolith-based age determinations and tag-recapture programs indicate that Osmerus mordax has a maximum lifespan of approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years] when maintained at the cool thermal regime of 12 °C [T = 12 °C] typical of its natal lakes and coastal waters. This lifespan is relatively short compared to other osmeriforms of similar body size, reflecting the high metabolic costs associated with anadromous migration and the elevated predation pressure encountered during spawning runs. Mortality accelerates markedly after first reproduction, with very few individuals surviving beyond their fourth or fifth year in heavily fished systems. The oldest verified individuals, usually from unexploited northern populations, exhibit extensive scale erosion and reduced condition factor. These senescent fish show declining fecundity and reduced swimming performance, ultimately succumbing to natural causes such as starvation, disease, or osmotic stress during post-spawn recovery.
